title: Latency drift and kernel stacking — timeline snapshot
content:
Purpose: capture a focused lab run that reproduces steady latency drift observed in a mixed-batch decoder workload. This is raw investigator notes + timeline exports from sampling Nsight sessions and a few short scripts that translate CUDA graph replay order into human-readable stacks.

High-level summary:
- Symptom: 95th/99th tail slowly increases over a 30–90 minute window under steady qps, even though model variant and batch target unchanged.
- Hypothesis: periodic kernel stacking and serialization introduced by CUDA Graph replay ordering + host-side launch jitter cause micro-epochs where SM occupancy collapses for a subset of microbatches, increasing tail latency.
- Key evidence: timeline slices show repeated clusters where small kernels (softmax, layernorm) are pushed onto a single stream, then fused by the graph replayer in a way that increases per-kernel latency due to reduced concurrency.

Environment:
- HW: nVidia A100-SXM (PCIe-less cluster), driver 525.85, CUDA 12.1.
- Runtime: serving-runtime v0.31.2-rc, cuda-graph-replayer experimental flag on (replay-mode=batched-compact).
- Model: decoder-only 8B, seq len 512, microbatch target 8 tokens, dynamic KV cache enabled.
- Load: steady 120 req/s, 40% 1-token, remainder 5–20 token responses.
- Nsight capture: short 15s snapshots every 10 minutes, host trace + kernel timeline + SM efficiency counters.

What I captured (artifacts):
- TIMELINE_EXPORT_2026-09-15_10-12.json (compressed): per-kernel start/end times + stream id.
- REPLAYER_TRACE_10-12.txt: cudaGraph node replay order and host submission timestamps.
- nsight-10-12-snapshot.ses (original) + timeline PNGs exported.

Observations (raw):
1) Periodic clustering: every ~7–9 minutes we see a ~20–30 second window where the number of concurrently active kernels drops by ~40–60%. During that window average occupancy falls ~15 pp (e.g., 78% -> 62%).
2) Short kernels elongate: kernels with nominal durations 60–120us were observed at 2–3x duration in the cluster windows. The serialized runs show these kernels executed back-to-back on the same stream rather than overlapping across streams.
3) Host-side replay jitter: host timestamps in REPLAYER_TRACE show small but cumulative offsets (~5–20us) between intended node replay and actual stream launch. When offsets align across many nodes, the replayer effectively serializes previously overlappable kernels.
4) SM stalls correlate with memcopy start times: small async copies (host->device) coincide with kernel clusters; NVLink/PCIe scheduling contention might shift DMA windows and alter kernel launch timing.
5) KV cache prefetch jobs sometimes run on default stream and create small gaps where compute kernels cannot overlap.

Quick metrics snapshot (representative window):
- normal window: occupancy 76.9%; SM active 88%; IPC 2.4; avg kernel duration 95us; 95th latency 32ms.
- cluster window: occupancy 61.8%; SM active 73%; IPC 1.9; avg kernel duration 185us; 95th latency 68ms.

Repro steps I used:
- Start a controlled load generator pinned to a single host CPU core.
- Enable timeline sampling in runtime (1s sample interval) and run replayer in batched-compact mode.
- Capture Nsight sessions for 15s at 10-minute intervals.
- Run a small analyzer that groups kernels by function name and stream id, and computes overlap windows.

Root-cause candidates (ranked):
A) CUDA Graph replayer heuristic (batched-compact) that attempts to minimize node count by serializing nodes on a single stream. Good for latency average but causes pathological serialization when host scheduling jitter aligns.
B) Host-to-device async copy scheduling that occasionally preempts DMA channel windows leading to delayed kernel launches.
C) Runtime internal microbatch alignment: when microbatch boundaries shift (due to small variations in token counts), some kernels move to different streams unexpectedly.
D) Driver-side stream prioritization bug (older driver series has known issues around priority inversion under NVLink heavy traffic).

What I tried (experiments):
- Toggle replayer mode: batched-compact -> batched-concurrent. Result: cluster windows disappear in 3/3 runs, occupancy stabilizes but average CPU overhead up slightly ~3%. Tail latency improves.
- Force small async copies onto user stream (instead of default stream) via cudaMemPrefetchAsync wrapper. Result: reduces DMA-correlated cluster events but does not eliminate them; indicates DMA timing contributes but not sole cause.
- Insert micro-sleep (10us) between nodes on host submission path to de-synchronize launches. Result: mitigates but not acceptable permanent fix (adds overhead).
- Upgrade driver to 525.93 in one node. No measurable change in short run (need longer soak).

Immediate proposals / action items:
- Short-term (low-risk): default replayer mode to batched-concurrent for Dedicated pools where tail matters. Add config knob to toggle. (OWNER: Maya)
- Medium-term: implement jitter-tolerant replayer that spreads nodes over streams when host submission density is high. R&D ticket to prototype (OWNER: Luca).
- Observability: emit replayer node replay latency histogram to console logs and Console metrics; add an alert if 99th replay-latency > 50us over 5m. (OWNER: David)
- Kernel hygiene: audit all small async memcpy calls and ensure they use a pinned high-priority stream or use cudaGraphAddMemcpyNode with consistent stream binding. (OWNER: infra-team)

Open questions / unknowns:
- Is NVLink traffic from co-located jobs increasing DMA jitter? Need multi-tenant trace.
- Does the driver's scheduler have a corner-case where many tiny kernels are preferentially queued on a single SM cluster? Follow-up with vendor.
- Long-term cost tradeoffs: batched-concurrent reduces tail but may increase nominal token cost; quantify on Optimize.

Notes to self / rough todos:
- Upload REPLAYER_TRACE_10-12.txt to the PR and reference JIRA-RT-6789.
- Run a 6-hour soak on 3 nodes with batched-concurrent vs batched-compact and compare 99th over time.
- Add small microbench harness that simulates host submission jitter programmatically and validate replayer heuristics.

Slack refs and links: #eng-serving-runtime (thread on 2026-09-15 10:30), see slack thread thread_ts=1723867200.

Concluding thought: evidence points to the replayer heuristics interacting poorly with small, timing-sensitive kernels and DMA windows. Immediate mitigation is to prefer concurrent replays for latency-sensitive customers while we develop a jitter-aware graph compaction algorithm.

-- David
